'''Man's Country''' was a chain of [[Gay bathhouse|bathhouses]] and private clubs for [[gay men]] in [[Chicago]] and [[New York City]].

'''Man's Country/Chicago''' opened at 5015–5017 North [[Clark Street (Chicago)|Clark Street]] in Chicago on September 19, 1973, and held the title of Chicago's longest-running gay bathhouse when it closed in 2017.<ref name=":4">{{Cite book |last=Keehnen |first=Owen |title=Man's Country: More Than a Bathhouse |publisher=Rattling Good Yarns Press |year=2023 |isbn=9781955826419 |edition=1st |location=Cathedral City, California |pages= |language=English}}</ref><ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Keehnen |first=Owen |date=2016-10-19 |title=Man's Country for sale: Not your everyday piece of real estate - Windy City Times News |url=https://www.windycitytimes.com/lgbt/Mans-Country-for-sale-Not-your-everyday-piece-of-real-estate/56878.html |access-date=2023-09-18 |website=[[Windy City Times]]}}</ref>

Less is known about '''Man's Country/New York''', located at 28 West 15th Street (originally 53-55 Pierrepont Street), which closed in 1983.

== History ==

=== Chicago ===

[[File:Architectural neon art from Man's Country (Chicago, Illinois).jpg|thumb|Architectural neon art from a hallway in Man's Country in Chicago (1970s)]]

Man's Country/Chicago was the third bathhouse co-founded by [[Chuck Renslow]]—a pioneering figure in [[LGBT culture in Chicago|Chicago's gay community]]—whose previous two clubs were forced to shut down due to [[homophobia]]-fueled pressure from the [[Chicago Police Department|police]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Miles |first=Bryan |date=2017-08-06 |title=Chicago Bathhouses: Sanitation, Sex And Sweat |url=https://www.wbez.org/stories/chicago-bathhouses-more-than-a-century-of-sanitation-sex-and-sweat/375cfc2d-0363-481b-992f-55b415bfd581 |access-date=2023-09-18 |website=[[WBEZ]] |language=en}}</ref> Before opening Man's Country/Chicago, Renslow co-founded a Chicago location of the [[Club Baths]] chain with Chuck Fleck.<ref name=":4" />

Man's Country was not only a bathhouse but also a concert venue, dance club, community space, gym, and sex club.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |last=Keehnen |first=Owen |date=2012-09-13 |title=If These Walls Could Talk: Man's Country anniversary - Windy City Times News |url=https://www.windycitytimes.com/lgbt/If-These-Walls-Could-Talk-Mans-Country-anniversary/39510.html |access-date=2024-01-26 |website=[[Windy City Times]]}}</ref> Renslow and his partner [[Dom Orejudos]] purchased the building on Clark Street in 1972 and performed significant renovations to convert it into Man's Country.<ref name=":9" /><ref name=":10" /> The three-story complex included a steam room, whirlpool hot tub, and sauna in the basement; a ballroom with a 30-foot ceiling and stage (part of the building's original design as a lodge for a Swedish social club); 26 private rooms; two lounges; a sundeck; a weight room; a juice bar; and various [[Kink (sexuality)|kink]] play areas for [[Cruising for sex|cruising]], including [[glory hole]] rooms.<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" /> Its basement wet area was designed to look like the [[Paris sewers]].<ref name=":9">{{Cite web |title=Our History |url=https://www.manscountrychicago.com/history/ourhistory.html |access-date=2023-09-18 |website=Man's Country}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Gettinger |first=Aaron |date=2017-11-29 |title=Facing Closure, Chicago's Oldest Bathhouse Throws Epic Party for the Ages |url=https://www.advocate.com/love-and-sex/2017/11/29/facing-closure-chicagos-oldest-bathhouse-throws-epic-party-ages |access-date=2023-09-18 |website=[[The Advocate (magazine)|The Advocate]] |language=en}}</ref>

The club's popularity peaked in the 1970s and early 1980s. [[Rudolf Nureyev]] and [[Wayland Flowers]] are among several famous patrons.<ref name=":5" />

Business declined as the [[HIV/AIDS crisis]] began to devastate the gay community in the mid-1980s. Renslow implemented numerous safety measures, including closing the orgy room and glory holes; distributing condoms and [[safe sex]] literature; and coordinating with the Chicago Department of Public Health.<ref name=":5" />

A dance club was added in 1987, but as the AIDS crisis subsided, patrons increasingly frequented Man's Country for sex rather than dancing or socializing. Famous entertainers who performed at the club include [[Grace Jones]], [[Boy George]], [[Charles Pierce (female impersonator)|Charles Pierce]], the [[Village People]], [[Viola Wills]], [[Pamala Stanley|Pamela Stanley]], [[Bette Midler]], [[Barry Manilow]], [[The Manhattan Transfer]], [[Sally Rand]], [[Divine (performer)|Divine]] [[Thelma Houston]], and [[Bruce Vilanch]].<ref name=":9" /><ref name=":4" /><ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /><ref name=":10">{{Cite web |last=Godfrey |first=Alex |date=2010-08-16 |title=Man's Country: A Man's Club For Men |url=https://www.vice.com/en/article/mans-country-a-mans-club-for-men/ |access-date=2023-09-18 |website=[[Vice (magazine)|Vice]] |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":2" />

In the early 2010s the club stopped generating a profit, which the owners attributed to the cost of increasing property taxes, insurance, and deferred maintenance.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":3" /> The club was put up for sale in 2016 but failed to attract a buyer. After Renslow died in June 2017, the decision was made to close at the end of the year.<ref name=":1" /> A raucous 13-hour party called "Loose Ends" was held on New Year's Eve 2018 to celebrate the club and mark its closure.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |last1=Gettinger |first1=Aaron |last2=Sowacke |first2=Brittany |date=2018-01-04 |title=Last night at Man's Country |url=http://chicagoreader.com/arts-culture/last-night-at-mans-country/ |access-date=2023-09-18 |website=[[Chicago Reader]] |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Loose Ends: The Man's Country Closing Party at Man's Country, Chicago (2017) |url=https://ra.co/events/1047399 |access-date=2024-02-11 |website=[[Resident Advisor]] |language=en}}</ref>

At Renslow's request, much of Man's Country's artwork and memorabilia, including murals by Orejudos (widely known by his [[pseudonym]] Etienne), was transferred to the [[Leather Archives & Museum]].<ref name=":2" /> The building was demolished in 2019 and replaced with a nine-unit condo building named The Renslow in his honor.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rodkin |first=Dennis |date=2018-01-23 |title=Condo building to be named for pioneering gay entrepreneur |url=https://www.chicagobusiness.com/article/20180123/CRED0701/180129964/andersonville-condo-to-be-named-after-chuck-renslow |access-date=2023-09-18 |website=[[Crain's Chicago Business]] |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== New York ===

| opened_date      = circa 1972
| owner            = Club Chain of Manhattan, Ltd.

| relocated_date   = circa 1978
}}

Chuck Fleck opened the first Man's Country bathhouse<ref name=":6">{{Cite news |year=1972 |title=Baths |url=https://digdc.dclibrary.org/islandora/object/dcplislandora%3A4189/datastream/PDF/download |access-date=2024-01-26 |work=[[Washington Blade|The Gay Blade]] |via=[[District of Columbia Public Library]] |volume=3 |issue=9}}</ref> in New York City before co-founding Man's Country/Chicago with Renslow.<ref name=":4" /> Man's Country/New York's precise opening date is unclear, but ''[[Washington Blade|The Gay Blade]]'' ran an advertisement for the "brand new" bathhouse in June 1972.<ref name=":6" />

The bathhouse originally occupied three floors<ref>{{Cite news |last=Phial |first=Frank J. |date=1973-09-24 |title=The Pierrepont: A Brooklyn Horror House |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1973/09/24/archives/the-pierrepont-a-brooklyn-horror-house-a-serious-annoyance.html |access-date=2024-01-26 |work=[[The New York Times]] |pages=37 |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> at 53-55 Pierrepont Street in [[Brooklyn]].<ref name=":6" /><ref name=":7">{{Cite web |date=2011-11-03 |title=You Heard It Here First |url=https://nymag.com/arts/books/features/love-goes-to-buildings-on-fire-2011-11/ |access-date=2024-01-29 |website=[[New York Magazine]] |language=en}}</ref> By 1978<ref>{{Cite web |date=1980-05-08 |title=Club Chain of Manhattan, Ltd. v. Christopher & Seventh Gourmet, Ltd. |url=https://case-law.vlex.com/vid/club-chain-of-manhattan-885844009 |access-date=2024-01-29 |website=vLex |series=74 A.D.2d 277,427 N.Y.S.2d 627 |language=en}}</ref> it had relocated to 28 West 15th Street in [[Manhattan]], where it occupied ten floors of a narrow building, leading to the marketing slogan "ten floors of fantasy."<ref name=":4" />

Amenities included the ''truck stop,'' a "full-sized red tractor-trailer cab [that...] was mostly the site of a continuous orgy;" the ''jail tank'', a mock holding cell; a Jacuzzi; and a restaurant called the ''Meet Rack''.<ref name=":4" /> The bathhouse also advertised its ''Satyr gym club'', rental lockers, and "low prices at all times."<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Green |first=Frances |date=Fall 1979 |title=Satyr Gym Club |url=https://www.abebooks.com/magazines-periodicals/Gayellow-Pages-New-York-New-Jersey-Edition/31311616031/bd |journal=Gayellow Pages, New York-New Jersey Edition |edition=1st |location=New York |publisher=Renaissance House |issue=12 |via=[[AbeBooks]]}}</ref>

Man's Country/New York once hosted a performance by the [[New York Dolls]].<ref name=":7" /> The bathhouse famously rented two large billboards above [[Hess triangle]] at 7th Avenue and [[Christopher Street]] that attracted photographers including [[Bettye Lane]].<ref name=":4" /><ref name="NYPL">{{cite web |author=Digital Collections, The New York Public Library |title=(still image) Gay Rights, Register to vote, (1978) |url=https://digitalcollections.nypl.org/items/9310de90-00b1-32df-e040-e00a18065ec5 |access-date=January 16, 2024 |publisher=The New York Public Library, Astor, Lenox, and Tilden Foundations}}</ref>

In 1978, Michael Rehak, a blind man, was refused entry by staff concerned that his blindness could constitute a safety risk in the event of a fire or other emergency.<ref name=":8">{{Cite news |date=1980-09-19 |title=Blind Gay Man Wins Bathhouse Discrimination Case |url=https://digitalassets.lib.berkeley.edu/sfbagals/Sentinal/1980_SFS_Vol07_No19_Sept_19.pdf |access-date=2024-01-28 |work=[[San Francisco Sentinel]] |page=9 |via=[[University of California, Berkeley Libraries]] |volume=17 |issue=19}}</ref> Rehak filed a complaint with the [[New York City Commission on Human Rights|City Commission on Human Rights]]. Man's Country/New York settled the case in 1980, agreeing not to discriminate against blind individuals and awarding Rehak a cash payment.<ref name=":8" />

According to Renslow, the New York and Chicago locations were managed separately and he was not involved in operating the New York bathhouse.<ref name=":4" /> However, [[:File:Man's-Country-Bathhouse-Chicago-New-York.jpg|a joint advertisement for both locations]] published in [[Little David magazine|''Little David'' magazine]]<ref>{{Cite web |date=2012-05-31 |title=Little David Shows Us What Was "So Gay" in Chicago in the 1970s |url=https://bijouworld.com/Gay-History/Little-david-shows-us-what-was-qso-gayq-in-chicago-in-the-1970s.html |access-date=2024-01-29 |website=[[Bijou Theater (Chicago)|Bijou World]] |language=en-gb}}</ref> and ''[[Chicago Gay Crusader]]'' in 1974<ref name=":5" /> suggests some degree of shared management, at least initially. Fleck later sold his stake in Man's Country/Chicago to Renslow.<ref name=":4" />

Man's Country/New York closed in 1983 during the AIDS crisis.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rhodes |first=Margaret |date=2020-01-23 |title=Where to Shvitz in New York |url=https://www.thecut.com/2020/01/shvitzing-spas-bathhouses-nyc.html |access-date=2024-01-26 |website=[[New York (magazine)|New York]] |language=en}}</ref>

== Cultural impact and legacy ==
* Man's Country/New York used its platform to advocate on behalf of the LGBTQ community, sometimes plastering its billboards with the messages "[[Gay liberation|GAY RIGHTS]]" and "REGISTER & VOTE,"<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ghaziani |first=Amin |date=2020-11-30 |title=Why Gayborhoods Matter: The Street Empirics of Urban Sexualities |journal=The Life and Afterlife of Gay Neighborhoods |series=The Urban Book Series |pages=87–113 |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-66073-4_4 |pmc=7978650|isbn=978-3-030-66072-7 }}</ref> as seen in [https://digitalcollections.nypl.org/items/9310de90-00b1-32df-e040-e00a18065ec5 this 1978 photograph.]
* A closet at Man's Country/New York once served as the headquarters of the [[Gay & Lesbian Switchboard of New York]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Martin |first=Douglas |date=1990-05-02 |title=About New York; Gay Dentists? Flirting Advice? Call the Hot Line |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1990/05/02/nyregion/about-new-york-gay-dentists-flirting-advice-call-the-hot-line.html |access-date=2024-01-15 |work=[[The New York Times]] |pages=Section B, Page 1}}</ref>
* At Renslow's request, much of Man's Country's artwork and memorabilia, including murals by Orejudos (widely known by his [[pseudonym]] Etienne), was transferred to the [[Leather Archives & Museum]].<ref name=":2" /> The Leather Archives & Museum was loaned a [[glory hole]] from Man's Country/Chicago in June 2019.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rhodes |first=Adam M. |date=2020-10-29 |title=Gay bathhouses were barely surviving. And then came COVID-19. |url=http://chicagoreader.com/news-politics/gay-bathhouses-were-barely-surviving-and-then-came-covid-19/ |access-date=2023-12-02 |website=[[Chicago Reader]] |language=en-US}}</ref> One of its neon signs is in the collection of the [[Museum of Neon Art]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-10-27 |title=Queer narratives in neon presented by The Museum of Neon Art |url=https://www.losangelesblade.com/2023/10/27/queer-narratives-in-neon-presented-by-the-museum-of-neon-art/ |access-date=2024-02-11 |website=[[Los Angeles Blade]] |language=en-US}}</ref>
* On May 25, 2018, the [[Chicago City Council]] voted to designate the eastern stretch of [[Clark Street (Chicago)|Clark Street]] between Winnemac Ave and Ainslie Ave—the historic location of Man's Country/Chicago, the [[Gold Coast (bar)|Gold Coast]], and other businesses owned by Renslow—as "Chuck Renslow Way".<ref>{{Cite web |title=Record No. O2018-3236 |url=https://chicityclerkelms.chicago.gov/Matter/?matterId=5F18AB4A-E10D-ED11-82E3-001DD80693B4# |access-date=September 18, 2023 |website=[[City Clerk of Chicago|City of Chicago, Office of the City Clerk]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2018-05-07 |title=Chuck Renslow street dedication May 19 - Windy City Times News |url=https://www.windycitytimes.com/lgbt/Chuck-Renslow-street-dedication-May-19/62799.html |access-date=2023-09-18 |website=[[Windy City Times]]}}</ref>
[[File:Mans Country Ad-Chicago Gay News-Journal 1977 Issue 13.jpg|thumb|1977 advertisement]]

== In popular culture ==

* Man's Country/New York frequently advertised on [[Channel J]]'s ''The'' ''Emerald City,''<ref>{{Cite web |title=Emerald City Tapes (Television Program) |url=https://gaycenter.org/archive-collection/emerald-city-tapes-television-program/ |access-date=2024-01-26 |website=[[Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual & Transgender Community Center|The Center]] |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-11-15 |title=The Emerald City |url=https://www.screenslate.com/articles/emerald-city |access-date=2024-01-27 |website=[[Screen Slate]] |language=en}}</ref> the self-proclaimed "world's first television show for gay men and women."<ref>{{Cite news |last=O'Connor |first=John J. |date=1977-06-02 |title=TV: Cable Focuses On Homosexuals |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1977/06/02/archives/tv-cable-focuses-on-homosexuals.html |work=[[The New York Times]] |pages=69}}</ref> (A [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Er1Ri3qKavw recording of one of its commercials] is available online.)
* The 2012 film ''[[Scrooge & Marley (2012 film)|Scrooge & Marley]]'' was filmed in part at Man's Country/Chicago.<ref name=":5" />
* In the 2014 film ''[[The Normal Heart (film)|The Normal Heart]]'', Ned and Felix first meet at Man's Country/New York.<ref name=":11">{{Cite web |last=Inoa |first=Christopher |date=2014-05-29 |title=NYC Film Locations for HBO's The Normal Heart |url=https://untappedcities.com/2014/05/29/nyc-film-locations-for-hbos-the-normal-heart/ |access-date=2024-01-16 |website=Untapped New York |language=en-US}}</ref> [[Matt Bomer]] and [[Mark Ruffalo]] take part in a recreation of a [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Er1Ri3qKavw real-life commercial] for the bathhouse.<ref name=":11" />

extract:
Man's Country was a chain of bathhouses and private clubs for gay men in Chicago and New York City.
Man's Country/Chicago opened at 5015–5017 North Clark Street in Chicago on September 19, 1973, and held the title of Chicago's longest-running gay bathhouse when it closed in 2017.
Less is known about Man's Country/New York, located at 28 West 15th Street (originally 53-55 Pierrepont Street), which closed in 1983.
